#10877. Working With a Marketing Agency: A Technical Guide for Developers and Designers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Sooner or later, most teams that build websites end up working alongside a digital marketing agency. The agency asks for CMS access, wants tracking scripts added, suggests URL changes, and sets targets for page speed. If nobody on the product side understands what is being asked and why, the result is broken analytics, accidental noindex tags, and migrations that quietly erase years of search visibility.

This guide is for developers, designers, and technical founders. It covers the engineering side of that collaboration: environments and access, analytics implementation, redirects, structured data, performance budgets, and crawler access, with code you can adapt and a checklist you can hand to whoever you are working with.

Marketing briefs rarely say it, but most outcomes are decided in the codebase and the design system:

That is why healthy collaborations look like a shared engineering effort with a reviewable change process, not a monthly PDF report.

Almost every painful marketing-and-engineering story falls into one of the patterns below. Each has a cause you can see in the code and a fix that takes minutes, if you catch it before launch.

Give the agency a staging environment and least-privilege access rather than production admin rights. Keep staging out of search results so test pages are never indexed. At the web-server level that can be a single header:

The risk is the other direction: that header reaching production. Add a post-deploy check to your pipeline so a launch fails loudly instead of silently:

Reports are only as good as the data behind them. Agree on a naming convention for UTM parameters before the first campaign, and document it:

For conversions, prefer explicit events pushed to a data layer over fragile click-based triggers. Developers implement them once, and every tool downstream can reuse them:

Test each event in your tag manager's preview mode on staging, and treat event names and parameters as part of your API: changing them is a breaking change that should be announced.

Changing URLs without redirects discards accumulated search visibility. Before launch, export every indexable URL, map each to its new location, and implement permanent redirects:

Do not rely on spot checks. This script reads a two-column CSV of old and new paths and verifies that each old URL returns a single 301 to a destination that returns 200:

Run it against staging before launch and against production right after. Redirect chains (A to B to C) and redirects that land on a 404 are the two failures it catches most often.

Structured data helps search engines and AI systems understand who you are. Generate it from the same data that renders the page, so it never drifts from the visible content, and escape it properly when you embed it:

Validate the output with Google's Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator as part of review, not after launch. If you would rather not hand-write the JSON-LD for every page type, free Schema Markup Generator can produce a starting point, which you should still validate with the tools above.

Ask for Core Web Vitals targets, and make sure marketing scripts do not break them. Google's published "good" thresholds, measured at the 75th percentile of real-user visits, are:

A budget nobody checks is a wish. Lighthouse CI can fail a build when a page exceeds one, which turns "please keep it fast" into a rule that applies equally to your code and to any tag the agency adds:

Sizes are in kilobytes and timings in milliseconds. Route every new tracking or advertising tag through code review and measure its cost before it ships.

AI-generated answers favor content that is clearly structured, factual, and easy to attribute. In practice that means descriptive headings, concise answers near the top of a page, accurate structured data, server-rendered content, and a deliberate decision about which crawlers may access your site. That decision lives in robots.txt, and it is an engineering and business call, not a default:

Check the documentation of each crawler you care about for its current user-agent name, since these change. If a vendor promises AI search visibility, ask exactly what they will change on the site and how they will measure the result. The field is young and claims are easy to make.

The following scenario is illustrative, not a real client story, but it combines problems that appear again and again. A team redesigns its site and changes URLs from /services/seo-audit to /solutions/audit. The redirect map covers the top 50 pages, so the launch looks fine. Three weeks later, organic traffic is down by a third. The cause is a long tail of 800 blog and resource URLs with no redirects, plus a CDN rule that rewrites trailing slashes and turns every single redirect into a chain of two hops.

Both problems would have been caught by the checks above: exporting every indexable URL from the sitemap and server logs rather than only the top pages, and running the redirect verification script against staging. The lesson is that migration work is mostly verification, and verification can be automated.

The best collaboration is the one that fits your stack and your team's way of working. Put the agreements above in writing, automate the checks that can be automated, and treat marketing changes like any other change to the product: reviewed, tested in staging, and measured after release. When engineering and marketing share the same process, the results tend to follow.

#10876. Introducing multi-backends (TRT-LLM, vLLM) support for Text Generation Inference

Since its initial release in 2022, Text-Generation-Inference (TGI) has provided Hugging Face and the AI Community with a performance-focused solution to easily deploy large-language models (LLMs). TGI initially offered an almost no-code solution to load models from the Hugging Face Hub and deploy them in production on NVIDIA GPUs. Over time, support expanded to include AMD Instinct GPUs, Intel GPUs, AWS Trainium/Inferentia, Google TPU, and Intel Gaudi.Over the years, multiple inferencing solutions have emerged, including vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, etc., splitting up the overall ecosystem. Different models, hardware, and use cases may require a specific backend to achieve optimal performance. However, configuring each backend correctly, managing licenses, and integrating them into existing infrastructure can be challenging for users.

To address this, we are excited to introduce the concept of TGI Backends. This new architecture gives the flexibility to integrate with any of the solutions above through TGI as a single unified frontend layer. This change makes it easier for the community to get the best performance for their production workloads, switching backends according to their modeling, hardware, and performance requirements.

The Hugging Face team is excited to contribute to and collaborate with the teams that build vLLM, llama.cpp, TensorRT-LLM, and the teams at AWS, Google, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel to offer a robust and consistent user experience for TGI users whichever backend and hardware they want to use.

TGI is made of multiple components, primarily written in Rust and Python. Rust powers the HTTP and scheduling layers, and Python remains the go-to for modeling.

Long story short: Rust allows us to improve the overall robustness of the serving layer with static analysis and compiler-based memory safety enforcement: it brings the ability to scale to multiple cores with the same safety guarantees more easily. Leveraging Rust’s strong type system for the HTTP layer and scheduler makes it possible to avoid memory issues while maximizing the concurrency, bypassing Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in Python-based environments.

Speaking about Rust… Surprise, that's the TGI starting point to integrate a new backend - 🤗

Earlier this year, the TGI team worked on exposing the foundational knobs to disentangle how the actual HTTP server and the scheduler were coupled together. This work introduced the new Rust trait Backend to interface current inference engine and the one to come.

Having this new Backend interface (or trait in Rusty terms) paves the way for modularity and makes it possible to actually route the incoming requests towards different modeling and execution engines.

The new multi-backend capabilities of TGI open up many impactful roadmap opportunities. As we look ahead to 2025 we are excited to share some of the TGI developments we are most excited about:

We are confident TGI Backends will help simplify the deployments of LLMs, bringing versatility and performance to all TGI users. You'll soon be able to use TGI Backends directly within Inference Endpoints. Customers will be able to easily deploy models with TGI Backends on various hardware with top-tier performance and reliability out of the box.

Stay tuned for the next blog post where we'll dig into technical details and performance benchmarks of upcoming backends!

Amazing work, looking forward to the releases!

This is so cool! Thank you for all the hard work.

That's amazing! It's going to be an awesome 2025 for TGI! 🤗

#10875. Timm ❤️ Transformers: Use any timm model with transformers

Get lightning-fast inference, quick quantization, torch.compile boosts, and effortless fine-tuning for any timm model—all within the friendly 🤗 transformers ecosystem.

Enter TimmWrapper—a simple, yet powerful tool that unlocks this potential.

To follow along with this blog post, install the latest version of transformers and timm by running:

Check out the full repository for all code examples and notebooks: 🔗 TimmWrapper Examples

The PyTorch Image Models (timm) library offers a rich collection of state-of-the-art computer vision models, along with useful layers, utilities, optimizers, and data augmentations. With more than 32K GitHub stars and more than 200K daily downloads at the time of writing, it's a go-to resource for image classification and feature extraction for object detection, segmentation, image search, and other downstream tasks.

With pre-trained models covering a wide range of architectures, timm simplifies the workflow for computer vision practitioners.

While 🤗 transformers supports several vision models, timm offers an even broader collection, including many mobile-friendly and efficient models not available in transformers.

The timm integration bridges this gap, bringing the best of both worlds:

One of the standout features of the timm integration is that it allows you to leverage the 🤗 pipeline API. The pipeline API abstracts away a lot of complexity, making it easy to load a pre-trained model, perform inference, and view results with a few lines of code.

Let's see how to use a transformers pipeline with the MobileNetV4. This architecture does not have a native transformers implementation, but can be easily used from timm:

Want to quickly create an interactive web app for image classification? Gradio makes it simple to build a user-friendly interface with minimal code. Let's combine Gradio with the pipeline API to classify food images using a fine-tuned timm ViT model (we will cover fine tuning in a later section).

Here’s how you can set up a quick demo with a timm model:

Here’s a live example hosted on Hugging Face Spaces. You can test it directly in your browser!

The 🤗 transformers library provides Auto Classes to abstract away the complexity of loading models and processors. With the TimmWrapper, you can use AutoModelForImageClassification and AutoImageProcessor to load any timm model effortlessly.

Quantization is a powerful technique to reduce model size and speed up inference, especially for deployment on resource-constrained devices. With the timm integration, you can quantize any timm model on the fly with just a few lines of code using BitsAndBytesConfig from bitsandbytes.

Here’s how simple it is to quantize a timm model:

Quantized models perform almost identically to full-precision models during inference:

Fine-tuning a timm model with the Trainer API from 🤗 transformers is straightforward and highly flexible. You can fine-tune your model on custom datasets using the Trainer class, which handles the training loop, logging, and evaluation. Additionally, you can fine-tune using LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to train efficiently with fewer parameters.

This section gives a quick overview of both standard fine-tuning and LoRA fine-tuning, with links to the complete code.

The Trainer API makes it easy to set up training with minimal code. Here's an outline of what a fine-tuning setup looks like:

What's remarkable about this approach is that it mirrors the exact workflow used for native transformers models, maintaining consistency across different model types.

This means you can use the familiar Trainer API to fine-tune not just Transformers models, but also any timm model—bringing powerful models from the timm library into the Hugging Face ecosystem with minimal adjustments. This significantly broadens the scope of models you can fine-tune using the same trusted tools and workflows.

Model Example:Fine-tuned ViT on Food-101: vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.ft_food101

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) allows you to fine-tune large models efficiently by training only a few additional parameters, rather than the full set of model weights. This makes fine-tuning faster, and allows the use of consumer hardware. You can fine-tune a timm model using LoRA with the PEFT library.

Model Example:LoRA Fine-Tuned ViT on Food-101: vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.lora_ft_food101

LoRA is just one example of efficient adapter-based fine-tuning methods you can apply to timm models. The integration of timm with the 🤗 ecosystem opens up a wide variety of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques, allowing you to choose the method that best fits your use case.

Once the model is LoRA fine-tuned, we only push the adapter weights to the Hugging Face Hub. This section helps you to download the adapter weights, merge the adapter weights with the base model, and then perform inference.

One of Ross' (creator of timm) favourite features is that this integration maintains full 'round-trip' compatibility. Namely, using the wrapper one can fine-tune a timm model on a new dataset using transformer's Trainer, publish the resulting model to the Hugging Face hub, and then load the fine-tuned model in timm again using timm.create_model('hf-hub:my_org/my_fine_tuned_model', pretrained=True).

Let us see how we can load our fine tuned model ariG23498/vit_base_patch16_224.augreg2_in21k_ft_in1k.ft_food101 with timm

With torch.compile in PyTorch 2.0, you can achieve faster inference by compiling your model with just one line of code. The timm integration is fully compatible with torch.compile. Here's a quick benchmark to compare inference time with and without torch.compile using the TimmWrapper.

timm's integration with transformers opens new doors for leveraging state-of-the-art vision models with minimal effort. Whether you're looking to fine-tune, quantize, or simply run inference, this integration provides a unified API to streamline your workflow.

Start exploring today and unlock new possibilities in computer vision!

We want to give a huge shout-out to the folks who made this integration happen in Transformers PR #34564. In no particular order, a big thanks to Pavel Iakubovskii, Ross Wightman, Lysandre Debut, Pablo Montalvo, Arthur Zucker, and Amy Roberts for all your incredible work. Your combined efforts took this feature from an idea to something everyone can now enjoy!

#10873. Check if eMudhra CA Is Still Trusted in Your Runtime

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Eight eMudhra intermediate Certificate Authority private keys are trivially recoverable from their public certificates. Any attacker can mint trusted TLS certificates for arbitrary domains. Browsers have already blocked these compromised intermediates through revocation mechanisms, but most non-browser runtimes — curl, Python, Node.js, Go, and Rust — still silently trust them. This affects any team operating server-side infrastructure, CI pipelines, or CLI tooling that makes outbound TLS connections. If your stack trusts the eMudhra chain, an attacker can forge certificates your code will accept without complaint.

This guide provides a diagnostic sequence: test every runtime in the stack against the compromised certificates, remediate by updating trust stores, and verify the fix sticks. The primary source for this disclosure is Scott Helme's detailed writeup.

In RSA key generation, you derive the private exponent d via the modular inverse of the public exponent e modulo λ(n) (the Carmichael totient of the modulus), where λ(n) depends on the prime factors of n. RSA's security depends entirely on d being large — typically hundreds of digits — making it computationally infeasible to derive from the public key alone.

eMudhra generated eight intermediate CA certificates with single-byte d values. Specific recovered values include d=4, d=56, and d=115, as documented in Scott Helme's disclosure post. These are not large numbers. They are recoverable from the public certificate in milliseconds. Anyone with access to the public certificate (which is, by definition, public) can reconstruct the private key and sign certificates that chain up to eMudhra's trusted root. That means arbitrary TLS certificates for any domain, indistinguishable from legitimate ones to any client that trusts the eMudhra chain.

An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

The practical consequence is total impersonation capability. An attacker holding one of these recovered keys can issue a certificate for any hostname, and any TLS client trusting the eMudhra intermediate will accept it without complaint.

Major browsers have deployed mitigations through their respective revocation infrastructure. The compromise was reported to Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, and eMudhra on Saturday, October 17, 2026. Chrome pushed a CRLSet update blocking the intermediates the same evening, Mozilla blocked them in Firefox via OneCRL within hours, Apple applied its platform block on October 19, and Microsoft rolled out a disallowed-certificate CTL update. Current browser versions already reject the compromised intermediates.

The problem lies everywhere else. Non-browser TLS clients skip revocation checks by default. curl does not check CRLs or OCSP unless explicitly configured to do so. Python's requests and urllib3 libraries rely on the certifi bundle and perform no revocation checking. Python's standard library urllib.request module uses the system SSL store, not certifi. Node.js's https module uses either a compiled-in root store or the system store depending on build configuration, with no active revocation. Go's crypto/tls loads system roots but does not perform revocation checks. Rust's rustls paired with webpki-roots uses a bundled Mozilla root set, while native-tls defers to the system store; neither checks revocation by default.

This creates a trust store gap. The system CA bundle on a Linux server, the certifi bundle shipped with Python, and the compiled-in roots in Node.js might all still contain the eMudhra intermediates or trust the root that chains to them. Without manual intervention, these runtimes remain vulnerable.

The incident's official test infrastructure, documented on the status page at emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com, provides twelve TLS endpoints: one for each of the six compromised TLS intermediates, served twice - once chaining to eMudhra’s emSign ECC root and once chaining to Sectigo’s cross-signing AAA Certificate Services root. Host names follow the pattern dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (eMudhra chain) and dv-g3b-aaa-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com (Sectigo cross-signed chain), with dv/ov/ev and g3b/g3c variants covering all six TLS intermediates. The diagnostic logic is straightforward: if a runtime connects successfully, it still trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. If the TLS handshake fails with a certificate verification error, the runtime correctly distrusts the intermediate. The bare domain emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com serves only the status page itself over an ordinary Let’s Encrypt certificate, so connecting to it proves nothing - always test the per-intermediate subdomains. Test at least one -emudhra host and its -aaa-emudhra counterpart: a store can distrust one root path while still trusting the other.

Important: A network or DNS error will also produce a connection failure. Before concluding SAFE, confirm the endpoint is reachable by running curl -v --insecure https://dv-g3b-emudhra.we-have-a-problem.com/ and verify that any TLS error is certificate-related (e.g., "certificate verify failed"), not a network connectivity error.

Run curl with verbose output against the test endpoint:

If the connection succeeds and returns an HTTP response, the system's CA bundle still trusts the compromised intermediate. Look for SSL certificate verify ok in the verbose output. If instead curl reports an error such as SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate or certificate verify failed, the intermediate is distrusted and the runtime is safe.

For a more granular view, use OpenSSL's s_client directly:

A Verify return code: 0 (ok) means the chain is trusted and the system is vulnerable. Any non-zero return code, such as Verify return code: 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate), indicates the intermediate is not trusted.

Each runtime below connects to the same test endpoint. A successful HTTP response means the runtime trusts the compromised chain and is vulnerable. A certificate verification error means the runtime correctly rejects it.

This tests the system SSL store only; urllib.request uses the system SSL context, not the certifi bundle. An ssl.SSLCertVerificationError confirms the intermediate is distrusted. Check the error message to confirm it references a certificate verification failure rather than a configuration or network problem.

A successful response here means the certifi bundle specifically trusts the compromised chain, independent of the system store.

If Node.js prints a status code, it trusts the compromised intermediate. A certificate-related error in the output means it does not. Whether Node.js uses its compiled-in roots or the system store depends on build configuration, so this test reflects whichever store your build uses.

Initialize a module first, then save the following as check.go:

Run with go run check.go. Go loads system roots via crypto/x509, so the result reflects whether the OS trust store has been updated.

Run with cargo run. With rustls + webpki-roots, the result depends on whether the bundled root set has been updated. With native-tls, the result reflects the system store.

Offline verification needs PEM chains for the eight compromised intermediates. The research disclosure site linked in Scott Helme's post at https://scotthelme.co.uk/eight-bits-of-trust-emudhras-ca-keys-cracked-in-milliseconds/ is the canonical starting point for the incident's test material. Use only chains you have verified come from that source, save them as individual .pem files in a local emudhra-chains/ directory, and check their integrity against any checksum the researchers publish. Do not use copies from unverified mirrors.

The directory should contain one PEM file per compromised intermediate chain before you continue.

Use a shell loop to test each chain individually against the system CA bundle. The glob form (openssl verify ... *.pem) is unreliable across OpenSSL versions — multi-file positional arguments require OpenSSL ≥ 3.0 and can silently skip files on older versions. Use the loop instead:

On Debian/Ubuntu systems, the bundle is typically at /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. On RHEL/Fedora/CentOS, look for /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt. On macOS, the system bundle is at /etc/ssl/cert.pem, though Homebrew-installed OpenSSL uses its own path.

If any chain returns OK, the system store still trusts that compromised intermediate and is vulnerable. A verification failure means it is distrusted.

Python's certifi bundle location can be found with:

Node.js behavior varies: some builds use a compiled-in root store derived from Mozilla's NSS roots, while others defer to the system store. The --use-openssl-ca flag forces Node.js to use the system's OpenSSL CA store instead of its compiled-in bundle. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store. Verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca; if no output appears, the flag has no effect on that build.

Go's crypto/x509 package loads system roots at runtime, so Go programs inherit the system trust store. There is no separate bundle to verify.

Run a shell loop to verify all eight chains against the certifi bundle:

Any OK result means the certifi bundle is still vulnerable.

The following commands apply to specific distributions. Run openssl version first to confirm your baseline.

If the distribution has not yet issued a patch removing the eMudhra intermediates, you must manually distrust the certificates. The correct mechanism is distribution-specific:

After any manual changes, regenerate the consolidated bundle by running the appropriate update command for your distribution and re-verify with the shell loop above.

Important: Homebrew's CA bundle only affects Homebrew-linked binaries (e.g., Homebrew-installed curl, python3). System tools (/usr/bin/curl, Safari, system Python) use the macOS Keychain and require a macOS security update via System Settings → Software Update. You can verify which curl you are using with which curl.

macOS caveat: Apple’s October 19 platform block covers Safari and Keychain-based clients, but the built-in curl, git, python3, perl, and ruby verify against /etc/ssl/cert.pem without checking revocation, and that file has not been updated at time of writing. The incident status page publishes an official workaround that strips the two affected roots from /etc/ssl/cert.pem, plus a PIP_CERT fix for the built-in pip. Homebrew’s ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 is patched.

For the system Keychain, open Keychain Access and search for eMudhra intermediates. Apple's platform-level block propagates through macOS security updates, though exact timelines for older macOS versions differ. Older macOS versions that no longer receive security updates will never receive the distrust entry.

Verify the new version by checking pip show certifi and comparing against upstream release notes. Applications that pin an older certifi version in their dependency files remain vulnerable until that pin is updated.

For Node.js, upgrading to a patched release that includes updated compiled-in roots is the primary path. Alternatively, launching Node.js with --use-openssl-ca defers trust decisions to the system store, which you might have already patched. This flag only works on Node.js builds compiled with --openssl-use-def-ca-store; verify support with node --help | grep openssl-ca. Pre-built binaries from nodejs.org might not honor this flag. Different LTS lines will receive the updated root store at different times.

Go relies entirely on the system store, so confirming the system CA update has been applied is sufficient.

For Rust projects using rustls with webpki-roots, run cargo update to pull the latest version of the webpki-roots crate, which derives its root set from Mozilla's NSS. Projects using native-tls defer to the system store.

Rebuild container images with updated CA certificates. Pinned base images are a particular risk — they can lag behind security patches indefinitely.

CI pipelines using cached or pinned base images should pull fresh images or explicitly upgrade ca-certificates as a build step.

Electron's trust store source depends on version and platform. Consult the Electron documentation on certificate verification to determine whether your version uses Node.js's compiled-in root store or the OS certificate store — the boundary has shifted across major releases, and no single version threshold applies cleanly. Upgrading the Electron version or overriding certificate verification via the session.setCertificateVerifyProc() method are the available remediation paths. Verify the specific behavior against the Electron version in use.

Distrust at the intermediate level stops the current attack, but it is fragile: new intermediates cross-signed under the same root would be trusted by default. Mozilla has therefore gone further and removed the eMudhra root entirely in NSS 3.131.1, and Chrome has confirmed it is removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3, the root that signed the compromised intermediates, from the Chrome Root Store, with the change reaching devices from October 27. Note also that the compromised intermediates were cross-signed by Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services root, so a chain can build through either root - blocking only the eMudhra root path does not close the Sectigo one, which is why the incident’s official Linux workaround distrusts both roots.

The following shell script runs openssl verify against all eight chains and exits non-zero if any chain is still trusted. Drop this into a CI step or run it as a cron job.

Monitor the following sources for updates on CA trust store changes:

Browsers auto-protect through active revocation infrastructure. Everything else — server-side HTTP clients, CLI tools, containerized services — requires manual verification and remediation.

Browsers auto-protect through active revocation infrastructure. Everything else — server-side HTTP clients, CLI tools, containerized services — requires manual verification and remediation. The action sequence is: (1) test against the online diagnostic endpoints, (2) verify offline against local trust stores, (3) update all system and language-level CA bundles, and (4) automate the check in CI so regressions from image rebuilds or dependency changes are caught immediately.

#10872. Hugging Face and FriendliAI partner to supercharge model deployment on the Hub

FriendliAI’s inference infrastructure is now integrated into the Hugging Face Hub as an option in the “Deploy this model” button, simplifying and accelerating generative AI model serving.

Hugging Face empowers developers, researchers, and businesses to innovate in AI. Our common priority is building impactful partnerships that simplify workflows and provide cutting-edge tools for the AI community.

Today, we are excited to announce a partnership between HF and FriendliAI, a leader in accelerated generative AI inference, to enhance how developers deploy and manage AI models. This integration introduces FriendliAI Endpoints as a deployment option within the Hugging Face Hub, offering developers direct access to high-performance, cost-effective inference infrastructure.

FriendliAI is ranked as the fastest GPU-based generative AI inference provider by Artificial Analysis, with groundbreaking technologies including continuous batching, native quantization, and best-in-class autoscaling. With this technology, FriendliAI continues to advance the standards for AI inference serving performance, delivering faster processing speeds, reduced latency, and substantial cost savings for deploying generative AI models at scale. #10871. SmolVLM Grows Smaller – Introducing the 256M & 500M Models!

We’re excited to announce two new additions to the SmolVLM family: SmolVLM-256M and SmolVLM-500M. That’s right—256M parameters, making it the smallest Vision Language Model in the world!

We built on everything we learned from SmolVLM 2B while focusing on efficiency, data mixtures, and new design trade-offs. We are excited to introduce a pair of models that preserve strong multimodal performance in a fraction of the footprint.

This release comes with four checkpoints: two base models and two instruction fine-tuned models with sizes 256M and 500M parameters. These models can be loadable directly to transformers, MLX and ONNX, and we have demos for transformers and WebGPU (with ONNX). You can find all the models and the demo for this release here.

We're now reaching model parity with the SmolLM2 family (135M, 360M, 1.7B), so you have a complete set of smaller LLM + VLM combos to play with.

When we released SmolVLM 2B, the community response was fantastic: The model is very light weight, open-source and permissive, and easy to integrate into existing workflows. But we wanted to push this approach even further for people working with constrained devices, consumer laptops, or even potentially browser-based inference. That’s where our new 256M and 500M models come in. On the other side, for people trying to process huge amounts of data, these models can run at a fraction of the cost of the 2B model.

In the last year, we trained two 80B VLMs and reduced them to 8B. Then for SmolVLM we took the challenge of reducing that 2B. And what we learned was that we could push the frontier way further! We are excited to show that at 256M and 500M we can still get great performance. Our new 256M model is the smallest VLM ever released, yet it surpasses the performance of our Idefics 80B model from just 17 months ago.

With just 256 million parameters, this model stands as the tiniest VLM ever. Despite its small size, it packs a surprising punch. It’s more than capable on many multimodal tasks, including:

If you need more performance headroom while still keeping the memory usage low, SmolVLM-500M is our half-billion-parameter compromise. It’s significantly smaller than the previous 2B release yet manages to push scores on tasks like DocVQA and MMMU closer to the bigger models. We also found this model to be more robust to prompting, which makes it out-of-the-box better fitted for production. But both models do great when fine-tuned.

We have visualized the throughput gains across different batch sizes in below graph. Below numbers are throughput benchmarks ran on A100.

1. Vision Encoder Choices Previously, we used the standard SigLIP 400M SO vision backbone, the same one found in many VLM architectures. For these smaller models, we experimented with two setups:

We found the performance gap wasn’t big enough to justify the heavier encoder for our 256M and 500M models. So, we decided to go small on the vision encoder, too. As a bonus, the smaller encoder processes images at a larger resolution, which (per research from Apple and Google) can often yield better visual understanding without ballooning parameter counts.

Similarly to our previous release, we rely on The Cauldron and Docmatix with the addition of MathWriting to the mix.

The proportions of the datasets were adjusted to place a stronger emphasis on document understanding (41%) and image captioning (14%), while still maintaining a balanced focus on other essential areas such as visual reasoning, chart comprehension, and general instruction following. With this update the model is built on a strong document understanding basis and lets the door open to fine-tunes that will adjust its understanding of specific tasks.

We increased the pixel shuffle even more! Our new models encode images at a rate of 4096 pixels per token, compared to 1820 pixels per token in the 2B model.

To optimize the tokenization even more, we added special tokens to represent our sub-image separators in a more efficient way. This means that now instead of a string like being mapped to 7 tokens, it is mapped to a single token. We did the same for strings up to . This led to a sizeable improvement in the model's stability during training and quality of the results. More details were documented in this LinkedIn post.

SmolLM2 came in three sizes: 135M, 360M, and 1.7B. With the two models we are releasing today, we now have a complete set of smaller LLM + VLM combos to play with.

We also found that it's surprisingly easy to fine-tune and experiment. The team behind the ColBERT-like retrieval models have trained ColSmolVLM, delivering SOTA multimodal retrieval speeds with performance rivaling models 10x their size. SmolVLM makes it faster and cheaper to build searchable databases. We think the 256M model can become a great specialized model for many tasks. Find the link on how to use the new ColSmolVLM with the new SmolVLM models in Next Steps.

We partnered with IBM to build models for Docling. Their early results with the 256M model are impressive. Below are some early examples they shared with us. Stay tuned for more updates on this!

Newer SmolVLMs are working out-of-the-box with the old SmolVLM code, so you can use transformers and MLX for inference and fine-tuning, and TRL for alignment 🚀 Moreover, this release also comes with ONNX checkpoints.

Get started with SmolVLM using transformers like below.

Use SmolVLM with MLX by running the following CLI command:

You can play with the WebGPU demos for the SmolVLM-256M-Instruct and SmolVLM-500M-Instruct.

Find links to fine-tuning and multimodal RAG with ColSmolVLM on the Next Steps.

We would like to thank ViDoRe team for training ColSmolVLM: Tony Wu, Manuel Faysse, and Joshua Lochner for the ONNX conversion and WebGPU demo and Vaibhav Srivastav for his help on this release.

#10870. Mastering Long Contexts in LLMs with KVPress

TL;DR: KVPress packs the latest KV cache compression techniques, enabling memory-efficient long-context LLMs. 🚀

One of the key features of Large Language Models (LLMs) is their context window—the maximum number of tokens they can process in a single request. As LLMs evolve, their context windows are becoming increasingly larger.

Larger context windows unlock incredible possibilities:

However, these extended windows come at a cost—memory taken by the long context in the KV Cache becomes hard to manage. For instance, handling 1M tokens with Llama 3-70B in float16 demands 330GB for KV Cache, rendering it infeasible for many applications.

In this blog post, we'll address one solution for this problem: compressing the KV Cache for more efficient generation. To achieve this, we'll explore:

Before getting started, explore KVPress in this Space (you'll find examples at the end if needed):

Figure 1: Key Value cache inside the attention module (Source: NVIDIA)

In autoregressive models, text generation happens token by token, with each prediction relying on all preceding tokens for context. For example:

This repetitive computation becomes inefficient as the sequence grows, especially for large models. KV Cache optimizes this process by storing the intermediate results—keys (K) and values (V)—from the attention layers, so the model can reuse them for future tokens instead of recalculating them.

As powerful as the KV Cache is, it comes with a major drawback-it scales linearly with the size of the context window. While this might not sound alarming at first, let's break it down to see why this becomes a serious bottleneck.

The values stored in the KV Cache come from all the attention blocks used by the model. Therefore, its size depends on the model architecture, which dictates the number of attention heads. More concretely, the memory consumed by the KV Cache is determined by the following equation:

Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers×nheads×d×ntokens \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times \text{precision} \times n_{layers} \times n_{heads} \times d \times n_{tokens} Size(KV)=2×precision×nlayers​×nheads​×d×ntokens​

Each of these factors contributes to the explosion in memory usage. To make this more tangible, let's consider a concrete example—Llama 3-70B running in bfloat16 precision (as recommended by the model authors) with a context size of 1M tokens:

Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB \text{Size}(\text{KV}) = 2 \times 2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1M = 327.6 \text{GB} Size(KV)=2×2×80×8×128×1M=327.6GB

Since bfloat16 uses 2 bytes per parameter, the model weights alone require 140 GB (70B x 2 bytes). This means that running the model with a 1M token context size demands approximately 470 GB of memory, with the KV cache alone accounting for a staggering 70% of this total.

As we've seen, the KV Cache is both a critical enabler and a significant bottleneck for deploying large language models (LLMs) with long context windows. Addressing the linearly scaling memory problem requires innovative compression techniques, and that's exactly where KVPress steps in.

KVPress, developed by NVIDIA, is a Python toolkit designed to address the memory challenges of large KV Caches by providing a suite of state-of-the-art compression techniques. It also integrates with other approaches, such as KV Cache Quantization, a method built into the transformers library to reduce memory usage (the precision term in the equation above), further expanding its utility (details here).

For researchers specializing in compression, KVPress offers a flexible and modular framework, making it easy to understand and extend with new methods. For developers, KVPress simplifies the process of deploying these cutting-edge techniques, enabling quick and efficient integration into real-world applications.

At its core, KVPress leverages presses, which are advanced compression algorithms specifically designed to reduce the memory footprint of the KV Cache.

Many of these presses rely on a score that is used in each head to prune the KV pairs with the lowest importance. For instance the KnormPress prunes the KV pairs with lowest key value norm (paper), and SnapKVPress prunes the KV pairs associated with a low attention weights for the latest queries (paper).

These presses are seamlessly integrated into the attention layers of the model using forward hooks.

Figure 2: KV Compression visualized (Source: NVIDIA)

During text generation, they dynamically compress the KV Cache, reducing memory usage without compromising the model's ability to generate coherent and accurate outputs. Each press is characterized by a compression_ratio attribute, which determines the degree of compression applied to the KV Cache.

These presses integrate seamlessly with a custom transformers pipeline, enabling easy application and experimentation.

Here's how you can use a press with KVPress with one of the many presses, ExpectedAttentionPress. This press prunes the KV pairs associated with the lowest expected attention weight for future queries.

Try using it directly in this Hugging Face space or in this Google colab notebook!

By targeting the pre-filling phase, KVPress ensures that the cache is compressed when it's largest—helping reduce memory overhead for sequences with tens of thousands or even millions of tokens.

The plot below demonstrates the GPU memory savings achieved with KVPress compression as prompt lengths increase. For shorter prompts, most of the memory is allocated to model weights—approximately 15GB for Llama 3.1 8B in bfloat16. However, as prompt lengths grow, the KV cache becomes a major contributor to memory consumption. For 128k context length, applying KVPress with a 50% compression ratio reduces peak memory usage from 45GB to 37GB. This smaller KV cache also improves decoding speed, from 11 tokens per second to 17 tokens per second on an A100 GPU (source). .

Figure 3: Memory usage vs Context length (Source: NVIDIA)

The research community has been actively developing various techniques for KV cache compression. KVPress encourages researchers to contribute their methods and already provides more than a dozen presses.

To evaluate the performance of these presses, KVPress includes a simple CLI for benchmarking them on standard long-context datasets such as RULER, InfiniteBench, and Loogle. The plot below benchmarks 9 different presses on the RULER dataset with 4k context length and different compression ratio. The best performing press on this dataset is a combination of the AdaKVPress (paper) and ExpectedAttentionPress, a new unpublished pruning technique created by the authors of KVPress (more information here).

Figure 4: Average score vs Compression ratio (Source: NVIDIA)

The growing context windows of LLMs unlock new possibilities but pose significant memory challenges with the linearly scaling KV Cache. KVPress addresses this by compressing the cache during the critical pre-filling phase.

While KVPress improves memory efficiency, higher compression ratios can impact model accuracy, as shown in the benchmark plot. Further research is needed to develop more effective compression algorithms that minimize trade-offs.

With its seamless integration into the transformers library and modular design, KVPress empowers researchers and developers to handle long-context LLMs efficiently and design new compression techniques. It's a practical solution for scaling LLMs without overwhelming memory resources—ensuring innovation stays accessible as models grow.

kvpress: LLM KV cache compression made easy

#10869. Prompt Caching API Example: Cut Token Costs in Node.js

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. For Node.js developers making repeated API calls with stable system instructions, few-shot examples, or long reference documents, prompt caching can deliver up to 90% cost reduction on cached tokens.

The problem is that three major providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — each implement prompt caching differently. Opt-in mechanisms, minimum token thresholds, TTL behavior, cache-hit indicators, and discount rates all vary. Developers must piece together incompatible documentation.

The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js. The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, TypeScript 5+, an API key for at least one of the three providers, and familiarity with async/await and REST API consumption.

All three providers cache from the beginning of the prompt forward — only the prefix qualifies. A "stable prefix" is any content that does not change between requests: system instructions, few-shot examples, long reference documents, or boilerplate context. Keep the prefix byte-identical across calls. Any mutation, even a whitespace change, invalidates the cache and forces a full re-processing pass.

Prompt design matters. Front-load all static content and append variable content (the user's actual question, dynamic context) at the end.

The following table captures the critical differences across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini:

For explicit caching, Gemini requires the largest minimum prefix at 32,768 tokens, making it suitable only for very large context windows. Gemini 2.5 and newer also enable implicit caching by default, which works more like OpenAI’s automatic approach. Anthropic offers the steepest read-token discount at 90%, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. OpenAI is zero-config but offers the smallest discount at 50%.

Update tsconfig.json with these essentials:

The CacheAwareRequest holds the provider-agnostic input shape. The CacheUsageReport normalizes the output so that calling code never needs to know which provider-specific field indicates a cache hit. The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate on cached tokens, while estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates actual savings relative to total tokens.

OpenAI caches automatically. There is no flag to set, no resource to create. The only requirement is that the prompt prefix must be at least 1,024 tokens long. The system message is the natural place for the stable prefix.

The systemPrompt string should contain the full stable prefix. As long as it exceeds 1,024 tokens and remains identical across calls, OpenAI will cache it automatically within its TTL window.

Anthropic requires explicit opt-in via a cache_control breakpoint. The breakpoint is placed on the last content block of the stable prefix. Everything before (and including) that block is cached; everything after is processed fresh.

The cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } annotation marks the boundary. On the first call, Anthropic reports cache_creation_input_tokens. On subsequent calls within the 5-minute TTL, it reports cache_read_input_tokens instead.

Gemini uses a two-step process. First, create a cachedContent resource via a separate API call, specifying the content and an explicit TTL. Then reference that resource in subsequent generateContent calls. The minimum prefix is 32,768 tokens.

Note: The GoogleAICacheManager class may be exported from @google/generative-ai/server rather than the top-level @google/generative-ai depending on your installed SDK version. If the import below fails, try import { GoogleAICacheManager } from "@google/generative-ai/server". Verify with: node -e "const m = require('@google/generative-ai'); console.log(typeof m.GoogleAICacheManager)" — if it prints undefined, use the /server subpath.

The cached content object must be stored and reused. If the TTL expires, the resource must be recreated. In production, persist the cached content name to a database or cache store to survive process restarts; the in-memory Map used in the factory below is lost on every cold start, causing redundant cachedContent creation and additional billing.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

The Gemini path stores cached content objects in a Map keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the full system prompt, avoiding both redundant cache creation on repeated calls and cache key collisions that could occur with prefix-based keys. A secondary inflight Map ensures that concurrent requests with the same prompt do not trigger duplicate cache creation calls.

OpenAI exposes cache data at response.usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. When this value exceeds zero, the request hit the cache.

Anthropic splits caching into two fields: response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (populated on the first request when the provider writes the cache) and response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens (populated on subsequent requests that read from it). Check whether cache_read_input_tokens > 0 to confirm a hit.

Check response.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount. If it exceeds zero, the cached content resource was used for that request.

The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate applied to cached tokens specifically. The estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates the actual savings relative to total tokens in the request — for example, if only 100 of 10,000 tokens were cached at Anthropic's 90% rate, the estimated savings would be ~0.9%, not 90%. The hash comparison across requests reveals whether the prefix changed. The token estimate uses a 1.3x multiplier on word count as a rough approximation (+-30% error); production systems should use provider-specific tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI) for precision.

Cache misses happen for several concrete reasons. You changed the prefix between requests (even whitespace or trailing newline differences count). Your prefix falls below the provider's minimum token threshold. The TTL expired — Anthropic's 5-minute default is particularly aggressive. You switched the model parameter between requests. Or, in Gemini's case, you did not pass the cachedContent name to the generation call.

Run with npx tsc && node dist/demo.js openai. Swap the argument to anthropic or gemini to test other providers. The first request populates the cache; the second reads from it.

Realistic savings depend on reuse frequency within the TTL window. OpenAI provides a 50% discount on cached input tokens. Anthropic provides 90% on cached read tokens, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. Gemini provides 75% for Gemini 1.5 Pro (the Flash rate is not confirmed at time of writing). Anthropic reports reduced latency on cache hits, but none of the three providers publish fixed latency benchmarks for caching; consult each provider's official prompt caching documentation for current figures.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

Start by adding streaming response support to the request-builder, since cached prefixes work with streaming on all three providers. From there, implement persistent TTL management for Gemini's cachedContent resources (which otherwise require manual recreation after expiry), and wire the cache usage logger into an observability pipeline like OpenTelemetry spans for production cost monitoring.

For full details on each provider's caching behavior, consult the official documentation: OpenAI Prompt Caching, Anthropic Prompt Caching, and Gemini Context Caching.

#10868. We now support VLMs in smolagents!

You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Matthew 7, 3-5

We have added vision support to smolagents, which unlocks the use of vision language models in agentic pipelines natively.

In the agentic world, many capabilities are hidden behind a vision wall. A common example is web browsing: web pages feature rich visual content that you never fully recover by simply extracting their text, be it the relative position of objects, messages transmitted through color, specific icons… In this case, vision is a real superpower for agents. So we just added this capability to our smolagents!

Teaser of what this gives: an agentic browser that navigates the web in complete autonomy!

🤔 How do we want to pass images to agents? Passing an image can be done in two ways:

For the case where we want to pass images at once, we added the possibility to pass a list of images to the agent in the run method: agent.run("Describe these images:", images=[image_1, image_2]) .

These image inputs are then stored in the task_images attribute of TaskStep along with the prompt of the task that you'd like to accomplish.

When running the agent, they will be passed to the model. This comes in handy with cases like taking actions based on long PDFs that include visual elements.

How to dynamically add images into the agent’s memory?

To find out, we first need to understand how our agents work.

All agents in smolagents are based on the singular MultiStepAgent class, which is an abstraction of the ReAct framework. On a basic level, this class performs actions on a cycle of following steps, where existing variables and knowledge are incorporated into the agent logs as follows:

As you can see, for use cases where images are dynamically retrieved (e.g. web browser agent), we support adding images to the model’s ActionStep, in attribute step_log.observation_images.

This can be done via a callback, which will be run at the end of each step.

Let's demonstrate how to make such a callback, and using it to build a web browser agent.👇👇

We’re going to use helium. It provides browser automations based on selenium: this will be an easier way for our agent to manipulate webpages.

The agent itself can use helium directly, so no need for specific tools: it can directly use helium to perform actions, such as click("top 10") to click the button named "top 10" visible on the page. We still have to make some tools to help the agent navigate the web: a tool to go back to the previous page, and another tool to close pop-ups, because these are quite hard to grab for helium since they don’t have any text on their close buttons.

For now, the agent has no visual input. So let us demonstrate how to dynamically feed it images in its step logs by using a callback. We make a callback save_screenshot that will be run at the end of each step.

The most important line here is when we add the image in our observations images: step_log.observations_images = [image.copy()].

This callback accepts both the step_log, and the agent itself as arguments. Having agent as an input allows to perform deeper operations than just modifying the last logs.

Let's make a model. We've added support for images in all models. Just one precision: when using TransformersModel with a VLM, for it to work properly you need to pass flatten_messages_as_text as False upon initialization, like:

For this demo, let's use a bigger Qwen2VL via Fireworks API:

Now let’s move on to defining our agent. We set the highest verbosity_level to display the LLM’s full output messages to view its thoughts, and we increased max_steps to 20 to give the agent more steps to explore the web. We also provide it with our callback save_screenshot defined above.

Finally, we provide our agent with some guidance about using helium.

Now everything's ready: Let’s run our agent!

Note, however, that this task is really hard: depending on the VLM that you use, this might not always work. Strong VLMs like Qwen2VL-72B or GPT-4o succeed more often.

This will give you a glimpse of the capabilities of a vision-enabled CodeAgent, but there’s much more to do!

We are looking forward to seeing what you will build with vision language models and smolagents!

Note: for the modal closing selectors please note that modals are also known as dialog elements and if built robustly should have a role="dialog" attribute in this is something that can be searched for when identifying these pop up windows.

In addition, any dialog/modal window should be closeable via the escape key as well!

Hope this helps identify modals/dialogs in a broader sense and/or helps close them out easier!

#10867. State of open video generation models in Diffusers

OpenAI’s Sora demo marked a striking advance in AI-generated video last year and gave us a glimpse of the potential capabilities of video generation models. The impact was immediate and since that demo, the video generation space has become increasingly competitive with major players and startups producing their own highly capable models such as Google’s Veo2, Haliluo’s Minimax, Runway’s Gen3 Alpha, Kling, Pika, and Luma Lab’s Dream Machine.

Open-source has also had its own surge of video generation models with CogVideoX, Mochi-1, Hunyuan, Allegro, and LTX Video. Is the video community having its “Stable Diffusion moment”?

This post will provide a brief overview of the state of video generation models, where we are with respect to open video generation models, and how the Diffusers team is planning to support their adoption at scale.

These are today's most popular video models for AI-generated content creation

There are several factors we’d like to see and control in videos:

With image generation models, we usually only care about the first three aspects. However, for video generation we now have to consider motion quality, coherence and consistency over time, potentially with multiple subjects. Finding the right balance between good data, right inductive priors, and training methodologies to suit these additional requirements has proved to be more challenging than other modalities.

Text-to-video generation models have similar components as their text-to-image counterparts:

The latest generation of video models shares a core feature where the denoising network processes 3D video tokens that capture both spatial and temporal information. The video encoder-decoder system, responsible for producing and decoding these tokens, employs both spatial and temporal compression. While decoding the latents typically demands the most memory, these models offer frame-by-frame decoding options to reduce memory usage.

Text conditioning is incorporated through either joint attention (introduced in Stable Diffusion 3) or cross-attention. T5 has emerged as the preferred text encoder across most models, with HunYuan being an exception in its use of both CLIP-L and LLaMa 3.

The denoising network itself builds on the DiT architecture developed by William Peebles and Saining Xie, while incorporating various design elements from PixArt.

It is possible to run any video model with extremely low memory, but it comes at the cost of time required for inference. If the time required by an optimization technique is more than what a user considers reasonable, it is not feasible to run inference. Diffusers provides many such optimizations that are opt-in and can be chained together.

Our goal is to make using these models easy and accessible. #10866. Open-R1: a fully open reproduction of DeepSeek-R1

If you’ve ever struggled with a tough math problem, you know how useful it is to think a little longer and work through it carefully. OpenAI’s o1 model showed that when LLMs are trained to do the same—by using more compute during inference—they get significantly better at solving reasoning tasks like mathematics, coding, and logic.

However, the recipe behind OpenAI’s reasoning models has been a well kept secret. That is, until last week, when DeepSeek released their DeepSeek-R1 model and promptly broke the internet (and the stock market!).

Besides performing as well or better than o1, the DeepSeek-R1 release was accompanied by a detailed tech report that outlined the key steps of their training recipe. This recipe involved several innovations, most notably the application of pure reinforcement learning to teach a base language model how to reason without any human supervision. As shown in the figure below, making a powerful reasoning model is now very simple if you have access to a capable base model and a high-quality data mixture:

However, the DeepSeek-R1 release leaves open several questions about:

These questions prompted us to launch the Open-R1 project, an initiative to systematically reconstruct DeepSeek-R1’s data and training pipeline, validate its claims, and push the boundaries of open reasoning models. By building Open-R1, we aim to provide transparency on how reinforcement learning can enhance reasoning, share reproducible insights with the open-source community, and create a foundation for future models to leverage these techniques.

In this blog post we take a look at key ingredients behind DeepSeek-R1, which parts we plan to replicate, and how to contribute to the Open-R1 project.

DeepSeek-R1 is a reasoning model built on the foundation of DeepSeek-V3. Like any good reasoning model, it starts with a strong base model, and DeepSeek-V3 is exactly that. This 671B Mixture of Experts (MoE) model performs on par with heavyweights like Sonnet 3.5 and GPT-4o. What’s especially impressive is how cost-efficient it was to train—just $5.5M—thanks to architectural changes like Multi Token Prediction (MTP), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) and a LOT (seriously, a lot) of hardware optimization.

DeepSeek also introduced two models: DeepSeek-R1-Zero and DeepSeek-R1, each with a distinct training approach. DeepSeek-R1-Zero skipped supervised fine-tuning altogether and relied entirely on reinforcement learning (RL), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to make the process more efficient. A simple reward system was used to guide the model, providing feedback based on the accuracy and structure of its answers. This approach helped the model develop useful reasoning skills, such as breaking problems into steps and verifying its own outputs. However, its responses often lacked clarity and were difficult to read.

That’s where DeepSeek-R1 comes in. It started with a "cold start" phase, fine-tuning on a small set of carefully crafted examples to improve clarity and readability. From there, it went through more RL and refinement steps, including rejecting low-quality outputs with both human preference based and verifiable reward, to create a model that not only reasons well but also produces polished and consistent answers.

This all sounds great, but what's actually missing? Let's have a look at the missing pieces of the puzzle.

The release of DeepSeek-R1 is an amazing boon for the community, but they didn’t release everything—although the model weights are open, the datasets and code used to train the model are not 😢.

The goal of Open-R1 is to build these last missing pieces so that the whole research and industry community can build similar or better models using these recipes and datasets. And by doing this in the open, everybody in the community can contribute!

As shown in the figure below, here’s our plan of attack:

Note that we don’t want to stop at math datasets. There’s a lot of potential in exploring other areas, obvious one like code but also scientific fields such as medicine, where reasoning models could have significant impact.

This initiative isn’t just about replicating results—it’s about sharing insights with the community. By documenting what works, what doesn’t, and why, we hope to save others from wasting time and compute on unproductive paths.

If this sounds interesting, we’d love your help! Whether it’s contributing code, joining discussions on Hugging Face, there are plenty of ways to get involved. Let’s build this together! 🚀
